claims.claim: Didymus the Blind was a fourth-century Alexandrian theologian and biblical commentator who lived from approximately 313 to 398.
Didymus the Blind headed the influential catechetical school of Alexandria.
Didymus the Blind was blind since childhood, having lost his sight at age four.
Didymus the Blind remained a layman all his life.
Didymus the Blind was a student of Origen and a loyal follower of his teachings.
Didymus the Blind was a leading opponent of Arianism.
Didymus the Blind's works were condemned by the Second Council of Constantinople in 553, not his person, because of his association with Origen's teachings.
Because of the condemnation of his works, most of Didymus the Blind's writings were not copied during the European Middle Ages and thus were lost.
The Fragments on the First Letter to the Corinthians constitutes the bulk of what survives of Didymus' 1 Corinthians commentary, with some remarks on chapter 16 also extant.

The commentary on 1 Corinthians 15 was written in response to beliefs and concerns arising from the Pauline text, including some in Corinth who said the soul was perishable and bodily resurrection was superfluous.
The Greek text of Didymus the Blind's fragments on 1 Corinthians was edited by Karl Staab in a 1934 edition.
